content.text:
I've read how localization works today. Here's the picture before I propose anything.

**Today:** `/planJerusalem/` is the only multilingual front-end (`site/planJerusalem/`, four locales — `en`/`he`/`ru`/`ja`, declared in `site/planJerusalem/i18n/translations.js:54`). The language is resolved at runtime by `initI18n()` (`site/planJerusalem/i18n/i18n.js`) in this order: `?lang=` → `localStorage` → `navigator.languages` → `en`. One URL, four possible renderings.

**Why that breaks Google specifically** — three separate failures, all from the same cause:

1. **One URL can only be one entry in the index.** Googlebot fetches `/planJerusalem/`, gets whatever its own `Accept-Language` produces, and that single rendering is the only one that can ever rank. The Hebrew, Russian and Japanese versions are not indexable at all — there's no URL to point at them.
2. **The translate offer reads a page that then changes under it.** The served HTML declares `<html lang="en">` with English static copy; `applyDocument()` rewrites `html.lang`, `html.dir`, the `<title>` and the `<meta name="description">` after load. Chrome decides whether to offer translation from the initial document, so a Hebrew reader gets an English page offered for translation which has already become Hebrew — or a page translated on top of a translation.
3. **Nothing tells Google the versions are versions of each other.** There is no `hreflang`, no `rel=canonical`, no `sitemap.xml` and no `robots.txt` anywhere in `site/`.

So I agree with your diagnosis — the language has to be part of the URL. The design decision left is which URL shape, and that one has a real cost difference here, so I'd rather you pick it than have me assume.

questions.question: Which URL shape should carry the language?

options.label: Subdirectory: /planJerusalem/he/
options.description: Google's own documented preference, and the one that lets each language ship pre-translated HTML (correct <html lang>/<dir>/<title> in the served bytes, so the translate offer and the crawler both see the real thing before any JS runs). Costs a small committed generator: four index.html files per locale with relative paths and static strings baked in, plus hreflang/canonical/sitemap. English stays at /planJerusalem/.

options.label: Query parameter: /planJerusalem/?lang=he
options.description: Smallest change — the parameter already exists and already wins over every other source. Google does support and index distinct query URLs with hreflang. But the served HTML stays English for every language (the swap is still JS), so the translate-offer half of the problem is only partly fixed and each locale's first paint is the wrong language.

options.label: Subdirectory for every locale, none bare
options.description: As above, but English also gets /planJerusalem/en/ and the bare /planJerusalem/ redirects. Fully symmetric, no 'default' language privileged — at the cost of a redirect hop on the URL that is already linked from site/404.html and anywhere else in the wild.

questions.question: What should the bare URL do for a reader whose device is set to Hebrew, Russian or Japanese?

options.label: Redirect to that language's URL
options.description: Keeps today's helpful behaviour but makes it visible: the reader lands on the localized URL, can bookmark and share it, and the address bar never disagrees with the page. Googlebot (which crawls without a language preference) still gets English at the bare URL, so indexing is unaffected.

options.label: Serve English, offer a switch
options.description: The bare URL always means English for everyone, including readers. Simplest and most predictable — one URL, one meaning — and Google's own guidance mildly prefers it to automatic redirection. The language picker in the header is how a reader moves, and their choice is then in the URL.

options.label: Redirect, but only once
options.description: Redirect on a first visit, then respect whatever URL the reader is actually on (a stored 'they have chosen' flag). Avoids fighting a reader who deliberately opened the English URL on a Hebrew device, which plain redirection does.

questions.question: Should the reader's language still be remembered in localStorage?

options.label: No — the URL is the only source
options.description: Once the language is in the URL, storage is a second source of truth for the same fact, and the two can disagree (a shared /planJerusalem/he/ link opening in Russian because that is what the visitor picked last week). Requirement 19.4 ('language and theme survive a reload') would need its language half rewritten — theme stays stored. Cleanest, and the only shape where a shared link reliably means what it says.

options.label: Yes — keep it, URL wins
options.description: Storage stays as a fallback for the bare URL only; an explicit /he/ or ?lang=he always overrides it. Leaves 19.4 intact as written, but keeps the ambiguity that a bare URL means different things to different people.

options.description: Google's own documented preference, and the one that lets each language ship pre-translated HTML (correct <html lang>/<dir>/<title> in the served bytes, so the translate offer and the crawler both see the real thing before any JS runs). Costs a small committed generator: four index.html files per locale with relative paths and static strings baked in, plus hreflang/canonical/sitemap. English stays at /planJerusalem/.
options.label: Subdirectory: /planJerusalem/he/

options.description: Smallest change — the parameter already exists and already wins over every other source. Google does support and index distinct query URLs with hreflang. But the served HTML stays English for every language (the swap is still JS), so the translate-offer half of the problem is only partly fixed and each locale's first paint is the wrong language.
options.label: Query parameter: /planJerusalem/?lang=he

options.description: As above, but English also gets /planJerusalem/en/ and the bare /planJerusalem/ redirects. Fully symmetric, no 'default' language privileged — at the cost of a redirect hop on the URL that is already linked from site/404.html and anywhere else in the wild.
options.label: Subdirectory for every locale, none bare

questions.question: Which URL shape should carry the language?

options.description: Keeps today's helpful behaviour but makes it visible: the reader lands on the localized URL, can bookmark and share it, and the address bar never disagrees with the page. Googlebot (which crawls without a language preference) still gets English at the bare URL, so indexing is unaffected.
options.label: Redirect to that language's URL

options.description: The bare URL always means English for everyone, including readers. Simplest and most predictable — one URL, one meaning — and Google's own guidance mildly prefers it to automatic redirection. The language picker in the header is how a reader moves, and their choice is then in the URL.
options.label: Serve English, offer a switch

options.description: Redirect on a first visit, then respect whatever URL the reader is actually on (a stored 'they have chosen' flag). Avoids fighting a reader who deliberately opened the English URL on a Hebrew device, which plain redirection does.
options.label: Redirect, but only once

questions.question: What should the bare URL do for a reader whose device is set to Hebrew, Russian or Japanese?

options.description: Once the language is in the URL, storage is a second source of truth for the same fact, and the two can disagree (a shared /planJerusalem/he/ link opening in Russian because that is what the visitor picked last week). Requirement 19.4 ('language and theme survive a reload') would need its language half rewritten — theme stays stored. Cleanest, and the only shape where a shared link reliably means what it says.
options.label: No — the URL is the only source

options.description: Storage stays as a fallback for the bare URL only; an explicit /he/ or ?lang=he always overrides it. Leaves 19.4 intact as written, but keeps the ambiguity that a bare URL means different things to different people.
options.label: Yes — keep it, URL wins

- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own — research it against the vendor's live documentation, capture what is portable as a technology skill with declared checks, and wire the project's use of it as a task in its structural local pack. Use when asked to make a repo do something with a technology nobody there has used yet (host it on X, send through Y, publish to Z), or to "research how to do this correctly" and "create a skill" for it.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- releasing-a-cloudflare-site: How a site served from Cloudflare is released — the version contract, the guards that stop a release loop or a half-release, forcing one, rolling one back, and which parts of Cloudflare only a person can change. Use when changing the release task, the wrangler config or the analytics loader, and when a release parks.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. Use when a revalidation sweep runs over a corpus of packs, or when asked whether a rule's environmental claim still holds.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- write-a-requirement-leaf: How a requirement leaf is written in the executable spec — the backtick-numbered one-liner with its detail collapsed under it, and which kind (surface snapshot, behavior, logic, saga, per-project, e2e singleton) its case takes. Use when adding or reshaping a requirement line in requirements.md.
- write-a-saga: How a saga case is written — a multi-step story captured as a golden storyboard or one animated APNG golden — steps, captions, frame budget, the real entry point, delay stripping and gesture marking. Use when authoring or changing a case under the saga kind.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, get the owner's approval of the plan itself — a line per step, the dependency graph, each link's automerge policy — before filing any of its issues, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. - writing-wiki-pages: How a product-wiki page is written and grown — the Key insights header, citation, what a source actually supports (attribution, independent voices, public proxies), correction without deletion, the growth log, sample-data, when a pass writes nothing. === assetsignore ===
# What sits inside the published tree but is not part of the served product.
# assets.directory uploads everything under site/, so this file — not a list
# kept somewhere else — is what holds these back. Gitignore syntax: wrangler
# matches with the `ignore` package, and a pattern with no slash matches at any
# depth while one containing a slash is anchored to site/.
#
# The tests live beside the code they test, which is where they belong; they are
# simply not pages. The Pages publish set shipped them — it named code
# directories wholesale and could not exclude a subdirectory — so dropping them
# here makes the live site smaller than it was rather than larger.
__tests__/

# The planner's static design mock and its notes: a prototype, never part of the
# product. The Pages publish set enumerated plan/ file by file to keep this out;
# this line is what replaces that enumeration.
plan/design/

# Documentation and tooling that happen to live next to the code they belong to.
plan/README.md
plan/package.json
=== verify.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# The repo's single verification gate: unit tests, JavaScript parse-checks,
# Python byte-compilation, and the Claudinite conformance sweep. Both the
# pre-commit hook (.githooks/pre-commit) and the pull-request gate
# (.github/workflows/ci.yml) run *this* script, and nothing else — so passing
# locally and passing on GitHub now mean the same thing.
#
# The conformance sweep is here because it was the one CI step this script did
# not cover, and the gap was not theoretical: a commit that passed `npm run
# verify` went red on GitHub for a blocking `claudinite-isolation` finding, and
# cost an extra round trip to notice and a third commit to fix. A gate you can
# pass and still break CI is not a gate. It is the slowest step by an order of
# magnitude, so it runs last — a syntax error should still fail in a second.
#
# Still NOT the whole of CI: `npm run test:ui` — the ui-requirements job, real
# Chromium against the committed goldens — runs beside this script rather than
# inside it. Green here means the fast lane is green.
#
# A few seconds and dependency-free — everything uses the node / python already
# needed to work on the project.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"

step() { printf '\n\033[1m▶ %s\033[0m\n' "$1"; }

step "Unit tests — node --test"
# The shared/ helpers both front-ends import, the Now page's own js/ tests, the
# planner's own tests, plus the local packs' — one glob for each pack's own
# pack.test.mjs (its checks' red-first fixtures), one for the shared task
# declaration test, one for the per-task tests beside each task. Those tests import
# every pack manifest and task declaration, so they are also what parse-checks that
# tree (the syntax sweep below deliberately stays off the .claudinite mount).
# Keep in step with the "test" script in package.json.
# product/requirements/ contributes its default-lane gates here: the coverage
# bijection, the gallery gate, and the pure logic cases. The browser-driven
# screen/behavior lanes are `npm run test:ui` (CI's ui-requirements job), not
# this fast path.
node --test site/shared/__tests__/*.test.mjs site/js/__tests__/*.test.mjs site/plan/lib/__tests__/*.test.mjs site/plan2/lib/__tests__/*.test.mjs product/requirements/*.test.js product/requirements/logic/logic.test.js .claudinite/local/packs/*/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/edfringe-now/tasks/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/edfringe-now/tasks/*/*.test.mjs

step "JavaScript syntax — node --check"
# Only our own tracked source: everything the site ships (site/), the scripts/
# tooling, the requirements harness and the design concepts. Never the vendored
# .claudinite mount (not our code) or the plan/design/ mock (HTML).
js_files=$(git ls-files 'site' 'scripts' 'product' 'design-concepts' | { grep -E '\.m?js$' || true; } | { grep -v '^site/plan/design/' || true; })
# `node --check` takes one file per process, and ~170 sequential node startups
# was the bulk of this script's runtime (4.5s of 7s). xargs -P fans them across
# the cores instead; -n 1 because the flag genuinely accepts only one path.
# xargs exits 123 if any invocation failed, which `set -e` turns into a failure.
if [ -n "$js_files" ]; then
  printf '%s\n' "$js_files" | xargs -P "$(getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN 2>/dev/null || echo 4)" -n 1 node --check

# Executable requirements — how this folder works

[`../requirements.md`](../requirements.md) is the numbered UI/UX spec; this
folder makes it executable. Every leaf id in the spec is claimed by exactly one
case here, and the committed expecteds (golden PNGs, coded assertions) are the
owner's approval record of the product. The framework follows the
`executable-requirements` pack standard; the judgment layer (doc-first,
owner-owned expecteds, re-baselining approval) is the `spec-driven-product`
playbook plus the `writing-tests` skill.

## Layout

```
product/
  requirements.md              the numbered spec (config.spec of the pack)
  requirements/
    coverage.test.js           the leaf ⇄ case bijection gate   (default lane)
    gallery.test.js            spec ↔ gallery-lines drift gate  (default lane)
    logic/                     kind: pure product rules          (default lane)
      logic.test.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js
    screen/                    kind: pixel-exact page states     (test:ui lane)
      screen.test.js cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js + <slug>.<id>.png (the goldens)
    behavior/                  kind: driven gestures, coded      (test:ui lane)
      behavior.test.js cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js
    shared/
      requirements-doc.js kinds.js cases.js     spec parsing + registries
      reference-now.js                          THE pinned instant + fakes
      png.js compare.js artifacts-dir.js        the pixel comparator
      render-case.js refresh.js gallery.js      render/refresh/gallery lanes
      case-helpers.js                           storage seeds, waits, drives
      harness/browser.js                        the hermetic Playwright page
      harness/vendor/                           Leaflet + web fonts, committed
      harness/vendor/systemfonts/               the font jail (see its README)
      fixtures/                                 the frozen dataset + builder
```

- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; a
  kind is added by dropping `<kind>/kind.js` + a runner — the loader, coverage
  gate and gallery all iterate the registry.
- **Goldens live beside their case**; failure artifacts (actual/diff) go to the
  gitignored `shared/.artifacts/`, never beside the goldens.
- **A golden is the smallest surface that proves its leaf.** A screen case
  declares its scope: `capture: "<selector>"` (a clip at that element's box),
  or `async capture(page, tools)` composing clips and stitches
  (`shared/capture-tools.js` — `element`, `clip`, `unionClip`, `stitchV/H`)
  for composites like one grid lane over three days with its label and pill.
  Omitting `capture` means full-page — a deliberate exception, not a default.
  The spec doc embeds these crops uncollapsed; the words stay folded.

## Lanes

| lane | command | runs | where |
|---|---|---|---|
| default | `npm test` / `bash scripts/verify.sh` | coverage gate, gallery gate, logic cases | everywhere (no browser) |
| UI | `npm run test:ui` | screen (pixel-exact) + behavior cases | pinned Playwright Chromium; CI's `ui-requirements` job |
| refresh | `npm run refresh:ui [filter]` | regenerates goldens + the gallery together | after an INTENDED UI change only |

The harness pins Playwright **1.56.1** (`shared/harness/browser.js`) — the
version whose Chromium rendered the committed goldens. The Claude sandbox
ships it globally; CI installs it per run; any other version refuses to
compare. Everything nondeterministic is faked once, in the harness: the clock
(Sat 15 Aug 2026 19:30 Edinburgh), geolocation (central Edinburgh),
`Math.random`, fonts/Leaflet/tiles/geocoder/data (committed vendor + fixture
bytes), CSS + WAAPI animations (frozen). Fonts go further than the web faces:
Chromium runs under a generated `FONTCONFIG_FILE` whose only font directory is
`harness/vendor/systemfonts/`, so the emoji and symbols the web fonts don't
carry come from committed bytes rather than from whatever the machine has
installed.

## The owner-approval contract

- A **golden** is owner-owned: an agent may *propose* one for a brand-new leaf
  (via the refresh lane), but never regenerates a committed one to make a red
  case pass. On a mismatch: surface `shared/.artifacts/<case>.actual.png` /
  `.diff.png` against the committed golden and **ask the owner** — refresh only
  on approval.
- A **coded assertion** (behavior/logic) is the expected itself — it is never
  weakened to pass.
- Refreshed goldens ride the PR diff, so approving the PR is approving the
  pixels.

## Adding a requirement

1. Add the leaf to `../requirements.md` (new number, a **one-line** statement,
   and a `<!-- req-gallery:<id> -->` line; anything not visible in the picture
   goes in a collapsed `<details>` Notes block). If the statement joins two
   claims with "and", it is probably two sub-leaves with two pictures. The
   coverage gate is now **red**.
2. Add its one case: `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js` — slug = the section's
   stable feature name.
3. For a screen leaf run `npm run refresh:ui <slug>.<id>` and get the golden
   owner-approved; for behavior/logic, write the `verify()` and watch it fail
   before making it pass.

## The fixture dataset

`shared/fixtures/data/` is a **frozen, curated snapshot** of the repo's real
committed data (provenance + the two documented adjustments:
[`build-fixtures.js`](shared/fixtures/build-fixtures.js)). It never tracks the
nightly data refresh. Re-running the builder re-casts every golden — that is a
deliberate re-baselining and follows the approval procedure above.

# Searching for a tool

- **A search that finds nothing** is evidence about your query, not about the environment: vary
  the query before concluding a capability is absent, and try the tool before telling the owner a
  step is theirs.
- **`select:` takes a short name as readily as a qualified one** — `select:get_teams` and
  `select:mcp__github__get_teams` both return the tool, and a comma-separated list loads several at
  once. Qualify a name two servers could both carry. (1)
- **A bare short name is a keyword query, and resolves too** — `get_teams` on its own returns the
  tool, ranked above the looser matches beneath it.
- **A server whose whole roster the deferred-tools listing already names** is the one exception: one
  miss there is the answer, so read the roster rather than rephrase the query.

input.title: Encode the Jerusalem planner's language in the URL
input.body:
The owner's report:

> the fact that the translations are all on the same URL causes problems with Google's automatic translation. Localization needs to be encoded in the URL.

## The problem

`/planJerusalem/` is the site's only multilingual front-end. Its language is resolved at runtime by `initI18n()` in `site/planJerusalem/i18n/i18n.js` — `?lang=` → `localStorage` → `navigator.languages` → `en` — so one URL serves four different pages. Three consequences:

1. **One URL is one entry in the index.** Googlebot fetches `/planJerusalem/`, gets whatever its own `Accept-Language` produces, and that single rendering is the only one that can rank. There is no URL that means "the Hebrew version".
2. **The translate offer reads a document that then changes underneath it.** The served HTML declares `<html lang="en">` with English copy; `applyDocument()` rewrites `html.lang`, `html.dir`, the `<title>` and the description after load. Chrome decides whether to offer a translation from the initial document, so a reader is offered a translation of a page that has already become something else.
3. **Nothing relates the versions to each other.** No `hreflang`, no `rel=canonical` anywhere under `site/`.

## The shape agreed with the owner

- **Subdirectory per language**, English at the bare URL:

  | | |
  |---|---|
  | `/planJerusalem/` | English |
  | `/planJerusalem/he/` | עברית, `dir="rtl"` |
  | `/planJerusalem/ru/` | Русский |
  | `/planJerusalem/ja/` | 日本語 |

- **No automatic redirection** on device language. Following Google Search Central's guidance — automatic redirection stops readers and crawlers reaching all the versions — the bare URL is always English and the header's existing picker is how a reader moves.
- **The URL is the only source of the language.** `localStorage` stops carrying it (the theme still does), so a shared link means the same thing to everyone who opens it.
- **The served HTML is already in its language before any script runs** — `lang`, `dir`, title, description and every static string — which is the half of this that actually fixes the translate offer.
- Each page carries a self-referencing `rel=canonical` and the reciprocal `hreflang` set, including `x-default`.

`?lang=` is dropped rather than kept as a tolerance: the page is days old and is linked only from `site/404.html`, so there is nothing in the wild to keep working.

- `19.6` Every translated string fits the pixel budget its key declares, in every language and layout.

  🚩 _Behavior leaf._ <!-- req-gallery:19.6 -->

  <details><summary>Notes</summary>

  A budget is a width in CSS pixels, per key — XLIFF 1.2's `maxwidth` with its

  renders: a clone of its own slot in the real page, under the pinned
  Chromium's own fonts, across every language and both committed viewports, so
  the number a translator is given is the number the browser will hold them to.
  </details>

- `19.8` Choosing a language in the picker takes the reader to that language's URL. 🚩 _Behavior leaf._
Notes The picker is the only way to change language now that no device preference and no stored choice do, so it navigates rather than re-rendering in place — which is what leaves the reader on an address they can bookmark and share.

# Fetching from the web

- **Needing exact text** — a summarizing fetch tool is not a source; when the bytes matter, `curl`
  into the scratchpad and read from disk.
- **A `403`** — don't retry and don't try a sibling URL; attribute the search snippet to the
  publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it for re-verification.
- **A sandbox or proxy denial is a policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around** — no
  open-network runner, no ad-hoc CI workflow, no push-triggered probe to make the request from
  somewhere the policy does not apply. Answer from committed reference material or ask the owner,
  and say plainly that anything unverifiable is unverified.
- **An explicit egress block** (`EGRESS_BLOCKED`) is domain-wide, unlike a publisher's `403`:
  working down alternate sources for the same fact spends the same denial on each. Never file the
  gap as "re-verify next pass" — no later agent pass can cross a policy block either; mark it as
  needing a human or an unblocked environment.

content.text: The transform isn't idempotent — it appends the derived attribute every run. Making it reset-then-apply:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("scripts/localize-pages.mjs")
s = p.read_text()

old = '''/**
 * Write every `data-i18n-<attr>` binding out as that attribute.
 *
 * The page does the same at runtime off `dataset`; from the markup the
 * attribute is simply the binding's own suffix. `data-i18n-slot` is not a
 * binding — it names the key an element's own code renders — so it is left
 * alone, and the bindings themselves stay in the markup because the page
 * re-applies them when the theme changes.
 */
function applyAttributeBindings(html, code) {
  return html.replace(/\\sdata-i18n-([a-z-]+)="([a-zA-Z][\\w.]*)"/g, (whole, attr, key) =>
    attr === "slot" ? whole : `${whole} ${attr}="${escapeHtml(t(key, code))}"`
  );
}'''
new = '''/**
 * Write every `data-i18n-<attr>` binding out as that attribute.
 *
 * The page does the same at runtime off `dataset`; from the markup the
 * attribute is simply the binding's own suffix. `data-i18n-slot` is not a
 * binding — it names the key an element's own code renders — so it is left
 * alone, and the bindings themselves stay in the markup because the page
 * re-applies them when the theme changes.
 *
 * A previous run's attribute is dropped before the fresh one is written, so
 * running this over its own output writes the same bytes rather than a second
 * copy of every label — which it has to, the default language's page being
 * both this generator's source and one of its outputs.
 */
function applyAttributeBindings(html, code) {
  return html
    .replace(/(\\sdata-i18n-([a-z-]+)="[^"]*")\\s\\2="[^"]*"/g, "$1")
    .replace(/\\sdata-i18n-([a-z-]+)="([a-zA-Z][\\w.]*)"/g, (whole, attr, key) =>
      attr === "slot" ? whole : `${whole} ${attr}="${escapeHtml(t(key, code))}"`
    );
}'''
assert old in s
p.write_text(s.replace(old, new))
print("ok")
PY

input.command:
git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Serve the Jerusalem planner's four languages at four URLs

The language was resolved at runtime — ?lang=, then localStorage, then
the device — so one URL served four different pages. A crawler had one
address to index for all four, and a browser was offered a translation
of a document that became something else a moment after it arrived.

Each language is now its own document. scripts/localize-pages.mjs
derives them from the planner's own index.html with every string, the
document's language and direction, its title and description already
applied, and maintains the canonical and hreflang block in all four. The
default language's page is both the generator's source and one of its
outputs, which is what leaves translations.js the only home of a string.

The URL is now the only thing that decides the language: no stored
choice, and no device preference — a page that redirected on the latter
would be a page whose other languages nobody could reach. The picker
navigates instead of re-rendering, so a reader ends up on an address
they can share. Storage keeps the theme alone.

The page's own asset and navigation URLs go root-relative, since the
markup is now served at two depths.

Refs #794

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vt5zuPsGYffecVAxeaoaqV
EOF

input.title: Serve the Jerusalem planner's four languages at four URLs
input.head: claude/vigilant-ramanujan-94i6ns
input.body:
Closes #794

The planner's language was resolved at runtime — `?lang=`, then `localStorage`, then the device — so `/planJerusalem/` served four different pages. A crawler had one address to index for all four, and a browser was offered a translation of a document that became something else a moment after it arrived.

## What it serves now

| | |
|---|---|
| `/planJerusalem/` | English, `x-default` |
| `/planJerusalem/he/` | עברית, `dir="rtl"` |
| `/planJerusalem/ru/` | Русский |
| `/planJerusalem/ja/` | 日本語 |

Each is its own document, **already in its language in the bytes the browser receives** — `lang`, `dir`, title, description and every static string — which is the half that fixes the translate offer, since a browser decides what to offer from the document it received rather than from what the page later becomes. Each names itself canonical and carries the reciprocal `hreflang` set including `x-default`.

**The URL is the only thing that decides the language.** Nothing is stored and the device is not consulted: following Google Search Central's guidance, a page that redirected on a device preference is a page whose other languages no reader and no crawler can reach. The header picker navigates instead of re-rendering, so a reader ends up on an address they can bookmark and share. Storage keeps the theme alone.

`?lang=` is dropped rather than kept as a tolerance — the page is days old and linked only from `site/404.html`, so there is nothing in the wild to keep working.

## The generator

`scripts/localize-pages.mjs` derives all four pages from the planner's own `index.html`. The default language's page is both its source and one of its outputs, which is what leaves `translations.js` the only home of a string — the markup's own English can no longer drift from the catalogue. `--check` re-derives and compares; `19.9`'s case runs that comparison in the default lane, so a hand-edit or a source that moved without a re-run fails the gate rather than shipping.

## Spec

Doc-first: `a40cc95` adds the leaves and leaves the coverage gate red, `e0f5586` makes it green.

- `19.4` loses its language half — storage carries the theme and nothing else.
- `19.7` the page speaks the language its URL names, whatever the device asks for.
- `19.8` the picker navigates to that language's URL.
- `19.9` each language is served as its own document, already in that language (table leaf).
- `19.10` each page names itself canonical and points at all the others.

## Verification

- `bash scripts/verify.sh` — green (7 pre-existing advisories).
- `npm run test:ui` — 117 pass, 0 fail. **No golden moved**: the two screen cases that change are re-pointed at the new URLs and render pixel-identically, so there is nothing to re-baseline here.
- Every new proof was seen red for the right reason before being made green — `19.9`/`19.10` against a page with a wrong `lang` and canonical, `19.7`/`19.8` against a `localeFromPath` that ignores the URL.
- Driven in a real browser off `python3 -m http.server` (which the harness's route interception can't tell you about): `/planJerusalem/he/` returns 200 with the programme loaded, root-relative assets and data resolving from the new depth; on an `he-IL` device the bare URL still answers in English, and the picker moves `→ ru → he → en` with `localStorage` empty throughout.

input.title: npm test warns MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON on every import of a site/ ES module
input.body:
Pre-existing, not introduced by any change in flight — filing it so it stops being tolerated silently.

Every run that `import()`s one of the site's `.js` ES modules from Node prints:

```
(node:…) [MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON] Warning: Module type of file:///…/site/planJerusalem/i18n/translations.js is not specified and it doesn't parse as CommonJS.
Reparsing as ES module because module syntax was detected. This incurs a performance overhead.
```

It fires in `npm test` (the requirements logic lane imports `translations.js` and `format.js`) and in `scripts/localize-pages.mjs`.

The warning's own suggested fix — `"type": "module"` in the root `package.json` — is not available: every `*.test.js` under `product/requirements/` is CommonJS and `require()`s its way around, so flipping the package type breaks the whole default lane. A real fix is therefore one of the larger options (a `package.json` scoped to the ES-module tree, renaming those sources to `.mjs`, or moving the test lane off CommonJS), none of which is a small cause-addressing change.

Worth noting alongside it: `.claudinite/local/packs/edfringe-now/RULES.md` currently states that the pinned Node 22 detects module syntax in a `.js` file "with no warning and no flag". The detection part holds; the "no warning" part does not, and the sentence should be corrected when this is resolved.

Done. [PR #795](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/795) → [#794](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/794).

**One correction I owe you:** I opened with `Comment class: other`. That was wrong — your message asked for a change to what a front-end does, which is this repo's `feature` class. The class can't be retracted, so `feature-requirements-first` was never armed; I worked doc-first regardless, because the spec demands it either way ([`a40cc95`](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/a40cc95) adds the leaves and leaves the coverage gate red, [`e0f5586`](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/commit/e0f5586) makes it green). No laundering — I'm naming it rather than back-filling a class.

```
site/planJerusalem/    The four served pages — index.html (English) plus he/, ru/ and ja/,
                       each already in its own language with its canonical and hreflang set.
                       i18n.js reads the language off the URL and stops consulting storage or
                       the device; the picker navigates instead of re-rendering. festival.js
                       gains the page root and its URLs go root-relative, since the markup is
                       now served at two depths.

scripts/               localize-pages.mjs — derives all four pages from the planner's own
                       index.html and maintains their canonical/hreflang block. --check
                       re-derives and compares.

product/               requirements.md — 19.4 loses its language half; 19.7-19.10 added for
                       the URL, the picker, the served bytes and the crawler annotations.
```

Three things worth your eye on review:

- **No golden moved.** The two screen cases that change are just re-pointed at the new URLs and render pixel-identically — 117 UI cases pass with nothing to re-baseline.
- **The English page is now generated too.** It's both the generator's source and one of its outputs, which makes `translations.js` the only home of a string — the markup's hand-written English can no longer drift from the catalogue. It also means editing English copy directly in `index.html` won't stick; the catalogue is where it goes.
- **On the decision you left to industry standards:** Google Search Central advises against automatic redirection on device language, so the bare URL is always English and the picker is how a reader moves. Verified live in a browser: on an `he-IL` device `/planJerusalem/` still answers in English, and `localStorage` stays empty across `→ ru → he → en`.

I also filed [#796](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/796) for a pre-existing `npm test` warning I hit along the way (unrelated to this change; its real fix is larger than a drive-by).

> ⚠️ Still open: [#795](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/795) is waiting on your review — CI hasn't reported yet, and I'll act on its events as they arrive. Not covered by this change: the site still has no `sitemap.xml` or `robots.txt`, so the new URLs are discoverable only via `hreflang` and the picker; say the word if you want those too.

A playable prototype of the illustrated trip planner (design-concepts/trip-planner):
the Postcard direction's opening and question cards, a calendar draft with vertical
day columns, and peel-to-correct tickets — running on committed test data for a
handful of cities, festivals, shows, restaurants, stays, transport modes and day
trips, so the experience can be played with before any of it touches live data.

input.title: Serve the Jerusalem planner's four languages at four URLs, and tell a crawler about them
input.body:
Closes #794

The planner's language was resolved at runtime — `?lang=`, then `localStorage`, then the device — so `/planJerusalem/` served four different pages. A crawler had one address to index for all four, and a browser was offered a translation of a document that became something else a moment after it arrived.

## What it serves now

| | |
|---|---|
| `/planJerusalem/` | English, `x-default` |
| `/planJerusalem/he/` | עברית, `dir="rtl"` |
| `/planJerusalem/ru/` | Русский |
| `/planJerusalem/ja/` | 日本語 |

Each is its own document, **already in its language in the bytes the browser receives** — `lang`, `dir`, title, description and every static string — which is the half that fixes the translate offer, since a browser decides what to offer from the document it received rather than from what the page later becomes. Each names itself canonical and carries the reciprocal `hreflang` set including `x-default`.

**The URL is the only thing that decides the language.** Nothing is stored and the device is not consulted: following Google Search Central's guidance, a page that redirected on a device preference is a page whose other languages no reader and no crawler can reach. The header picker navigates instead of re-rendering, so a reader ends up on an address they can bookmark and share. Storage keeps the theme alone.

`?lang=` is dropped rather than kept as a tolerance — the page is days old and linked only from `site/404.html`, so there is nothing in the wild to keep working.

## `sitemap.xml` and `robots.txt`

**These are not optional extras for a public website — they are the baseline both Google and Bing document as expected of any site that wants to be found, and the site had neither.** Google Search Central states a sitemap is recommended for every site (and effectively required for a site whose pages are not all reachable by link from the home page), and that `robots.txt` is where a crawler expects to be told where the sitemap is. `hreflang` alone would have left the three new language URLs discoverable only by annotation; with the sitemap they are stated outright.

The site now serves both, generated from the published tree rather than kept by hand:

- **`sitemap.xml`** — the 9 pages wrangler uploads for a reader, each at the URL the site's `auto-trailing-slash` handling actually serves it at, with the planner's four languages carrying `xhtml:link` alternates. No `lastmod`, `changefreq` or `priority`: nothing here could keep a `lastmod` true, and a stale one is worth less than none (Google ignores the other two outright).
- **`robots.txt`** — `User-agent: *` / `Allow: /` and the `Sitemap:` line, which is the only reason the file exists here. Nothing is disallowed on purpose: a `Disallow` keeps a crawler out without keeping the URL out of results, which is the opposite of what a page that must not be listed needs.

**What stays out says so on its own page.** The trip-planner prototype at `/plan2/` runs on invented data, so it gains a `noindex` meta; `site/404.html` already carried one. That meta *is* the rule — the sitemap lists every published page that doesn't carry it — so there is no second list beside the sitemap for anyone to keep in step, and a page added to the site is described without anyone remembering to come here.

`scripts/published-site.mjs` now holds the origin and the published page set, so the canonical, the `hreflang` and the sitemap entry are one answer rather than three copies of it.

No pack owns sitemap/robots plumbing yet — this is the first copy in the fleet rather than a third, so it is authored here; `public-website` looks like its eventual home.

## The localization generator

`scripts/localize-pages.mjs` derives all four language pages from the planner's own `index.html`. The default language's page is both its source and one of its outputs, which is what leaves `translations.js` the only home of a string — the markup's own English can no longer drift from the catalogue. `--check` re-derives and compares; `19.9` runs that comparison in the default lane, as `20.1` and `20.4` do for the sitemap and robots.txt, so a hand-edit or a source that moved without a re-run fails the gate rather than shipping.

## Spec

Doc-first throughout — each spec commit leaves the coverage gate red, and the commit after it makes it green (`a40cc95` → `e0f5586`, `fd0accc` → `ae97c64`).

- `19.4` loses its language half — storage carries the theme and nothing else.
- `19.7` the page speaks the language its URL names, whatever the device asks for.
- `19.8` the picker navigates to that language's URL.
- `19.9` each language is served as its own document, already in that language (table leaf).
- `19.10` each page names itself canonical and points at all the others.
- New **Part VI — what the site tells a crawler**: `20.1` the sitemap lists every page published for a reader (table leaf), `20.2` a `noindex` page is left out of it, `20.3` each language is listed with the alternates its own page declares, `20.4` `robots.txt` admits every crawler and names the sitemap.

## Verification

- `bash scripts/verify.sh` — green (7 pre-existing advisories).
- `npm run test:ui` — 117 pass, 0 fail. **No golden moved**: the two screen cases that change are re-pointed at the new URLs and render pixel-identically, and the prototype's new `<meta>` is invisible — so there is nothing to re-baseline here.
- Every new proof was seen red for its own reason before being made green — `19.9`/`19.10` against a page with a wrong `lang` and canonical, `19.7`/`19.8` against a `localeFromPath` that ignores the URL, and `20.1`–`20.4` against a dropped sitemap entry, a prototype with its `noindex` removed, a mispointed alternate, and an added `Disallow`.
- Driven in a real browser off `python3 -m http.server` (which the harness's route interception can't tell you about): `/planJerusalem/he/` returns 200 with the programme loaded, root-relative assets and data resolving from the new depth; on an `he-IL` device the bare URL still answers in English, and the picker moves `→ ru → he → en` with `localStorage` empty throughout. `/sitemap.xml` and `/robots.txt` serve as `application/xml` and `text/plain`, and the sitemap parses against the sitemaps 0.9 namespace — 9 `<url>` entries, 20 alternates.

Both files are in [PR #795](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/795), and the PR now states plainly why they're baseline rather than optional.

```
site/                  sitemap.xml and robots.txt — new, both generated from the published
                       tree. plan2/index.html gains a noindex meta: the prototype runs on
                       invented data, and that meta is also what keeps it out of the sitemap.

scripts/               published-site.mjs — the origin and the published page set, so the
                       canonical, the hreflang and the sitemap entry are one answer.
                       build-sitemap.mjs — writes both files; --check re-derives and compares.
                       localize-pages.mjs exports which page x-default names.

product/               requirements.md — new Part VI, section 20: the sitemap's contents, the
                       noindex rule, the per-language alternates, and robots.txt.
```

Three things to look at:

- **The exclusion rule is structural, not a list.** The sitemap names every published page that doesn't carry `noindex`. That means `/plan2/` and `404.html` drop out because *they* say so, and a page added to the site is described without anyone remembering this generator exists — `20.2` asserts the iff in both directions.
- **No `lastmod`.** Nothing in this repo could keep one true, and Google treats an unreliable `lastmod` as worse than an absent one. Same reasoning drops `changefreq` and `priority`, which it ignores anyway.
- **`robots.txt` disallows nothing, deliberately.** A `Disallow` blocks the crawl but not the listing — a blocked URL can still appear in results, with no description. `noindex` on the page is the tool that actually keeps it out, which is why the prototype got one instead of a `robots.txt` line.

One thing I'd flag for later rather than act on: sitemap/robots plumbing isn't owned by any Claudinite pack yet, so this is the fleet's first copy. If a second site ever needs it, `public-website` is where it should move rather than being written twice.

> ⚠️ Still open: [#795](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/795) is waiting on your review — CI hasn't reported since the push, and I'll act on its events as they arrive. Deferred, not done: [#796](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/796) (pre-existing `npm test` warning), and promoting the sitemap plumbing to the `public-website` pack if a second site ever wants it.

31	  join(PAGE_DIR, "i18n", "translations.js")
32	);
33	const { localeHref } = await import(join(PAGE_DIR, "i18n", "i18n.js"));
34	const { FESTIVAL } = await import(join(PAGE_DIR, "festival.js"));
35	
36	// The one hostname the site answers on, and so the one a canonical and an
37	// hreflang may name: an alternate that named a host the site does not serve
38	// would point a crawler at nothing. The wrangler config routes the apex here
39	// too, which is exactly what a canonical exists to consolidate.
40	export const ORIGIN = "https://www.edfringenow.com";
41	
42	/**
43	 * Every language this page is served in: what it is called, which way it runs,
44	 * the URL it answers on and the file that answers. One list, so the generator
45	 * and the requirements that check its output never disagree about where a
46	 * language lives.
47	 */
48	export const PAGES = LOCALES.map((locale) => ({
49	  ...locale,
50	  url: localeHref(locale.code, FESTIVAL.pageRoot),
51	  file:
52	    locale.code === DEFAULT_LOCALE ? SOURCE : join(PAGE_DIR, locale.code, "index.html"),
53	}));
54	
55	/** The page served at the planner's own URL, which `x-default` names. */
56	export const DEFAULT_PAGE = PAGES.find((p) => p.code === DEFAULT_LOCALE);
57	
58	const BEGIN = "<!-- localization:begin";
59	const END = "<!-- localization:end -->";
60	
61	const escapeHtml = (s) =>
62	  String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) => ({ "&": "&", "<": "<", ">": ">", '"': """, "'": "'" }[c]));
63	
64	/** One language's string for a key, in the language it is being written for. */
65	function t(key, code) {
66	  const entry = STRINGS[key];
67	  if (!entry) throw new Error(`no such translation key: ${key}`);
68	  const value = entry[code];
69	  if (typeof value !== "string") throw new Error(`${key}: no ${code} translation`);
70	  return value;
71	}
72	
73	/**
74	 * The canonical and hreflang block every language carries.
75	 *
76	 * Each page names itself canonical and lists every language including its own
77	 * — the reciprocal set a search engine needs to read four URLs as one page in
78	 * four languages rather than four pages competing. `x-default` is the default
79	 * language's URL: what to serve a reader whose own language is not among them.
80	 */
81	function localizationBlock(code, indent) {
82	  const lines = [
83	    `<link rel="canonical" href="${ORIGIN}${localeHref(code, FESTIVAL.pageRoot)}" />`,
84	    ...LOCALES.map(
85	      (l) => `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="${l.code}" href="${ORIGIN}${localeHref(l.code, FESTIVAL.pageRoot)}" />`
86	    ),
87	    `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="${ORIGIN}${localeHref(DEFAULT_LOCALE, FESTIVAL.pageRoot)}" />`,
88	  ];
89	  return lines.map((l) => indent + l).join("\n");
90	}
91	
92	function replaceManagedBlock(html, code) {
93	  const start = html.indexOf(BEGIN);
94	  const end = html.indexOf(END);
95	  if (start < 0 || end < 0) throw new Error(`${SOURCE}: the localization: block is missing`);
96	  const lineStart = html.lastIndexOf("\n", start) + 1;
97	  const indent = html.slice(lineStart, start);
98	  const head = html.slice(0, start + html.slice(start).indexOf("\n") + 1);
99	  // From the start of the closing marker's own LINE, so it keeps the
100	  // indentation it is written with rather than losing it to the slice.
101	  const tail = html.slice(html.lastIndexOf("\n", end) + 1);
102	  return head + localizationBlock(code, indent) + "\n" + tail;
103	}
104	
105	/**
106	 * Replace the text of every element bound with `data-i18n`.
107	 *
108	 * A bound element holds plain text and nothing else — no nested markup — which
109	 * is what makes this a replacement rather than a parse. That is asserted here
110	 * rather than assumed, so markup that outgrows the rule fails the build
111	 * instead of silently shipping a half-translated page.
112	 */
113	function applyTextBindings(html, code) {
114	  const open = /<([a-z][a-z0-9]*)\b[^>]*\sdata-i18n="([a-zA-Z][\w.]*)"[^>]*>/g;
115	  let out = "";
116	  let read = 0;
117	  let match;
118	  while ((match = open.exec(html))) {
119	    const [tag, name, key] = match;
120	    const contentStart = match.index + tag.length;
121	    const close = `</${name}>`;
122	    const contentEnd = html.indexOf("<", contentStart);
123	    if (contentEnd < 0 || !html.startsWith(close, contentEnd)) {
124	      throw new Error(
125	        `${key}: the element bound to it holds markup, not plain text — ` +
126	          "a bound element's content is replaced wholesale, so it cannot contain another element"
127	      );
128	    }
129	    out += html.slice(read, contentStart) + escapeHtml(t(key, code));
130	    read = contentEnd;
131	    open.lastIndex = contentEnd;
132	  }
133	  return out + html.slice(read);
134	}
135	
136	/**
137	 * Write every `data-i18n-<attr>` binding out as that attribute.
138	 *
139	 * The page does the same at runtime off `dataset`; from the markup the
140	 * attribute is simply the binding's own suffix. `data-i18n-slot` is not a
141	 * binding — it names the key an element's own code renders — so it is left
142	 * alone, and the bindings themselves stay in the markup because the page
143	 * re-applies them when the theme changes.
144	 *
145	 * A previous run's attribute is dropped before the fresh one is written, so
146	 * running this over its own output writes the same bytes rather than a second
147	 * copy of every label — which it has to, the default language's page being
148	 * both this generator's source and one of its outputs.
149	 */
150	function applyAttributeBindings(html, code) {
151	  return html
152	    .replace(/(\sdata-i18n-([a-z-]+)="[^"]*")\s\2="[^"]*"/g, "$1")
153	    .replace(/\sdata-i18n-([a-z-]+)="([a-zA-Z][\w.]*)"/g, (whole, attr, key) =>
154	      attr === "slot" ? whole : `${whole} ${attr}="${escapeHtml(t(key, code))}"`
155	    );
156	}
157	
158	/**
159	 * One language's whole page.
160	 *
161	 * The default language's page is the source AND an output: it is derived the
162	 * same way as the others, so the catalogue is the only home of a string and
163	 * the markup's own words cannot quietly drift from it.
164	 */
165	export function buildPage(source, code) {
166	  const locale = LOCALES.find((l) => l.code === code);
167	  if (!locale) throw new Error(`no such language: ${code}`);
168	
169	  let html = replaceManagedBlock(source, code);
170	  html = html.replace(
171	    /<html lang="[^"]*" dir="[^"]*">/,
172	    `<html lang="${locale.code}" dir="${locale.dir}">`
173	  );
174	  html = html.replace(/<title>[^<]*<\/title>/, `<title>${escapeHtml(t("doc.title", code))}</title>`);

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- deterministic-expecteds: What makes a rendered expected byte-stable — the pinned clock, faked inputs, real fonts, fixed-duration pumps — and the per-stack rendering recipe (jsdom+satori for DOM products, Flutter golden files) with pixel-exact comparison. Use when writing a case, the render harness or the fake world under dev/requirements.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- explore-link: Mine one given URL for product, market, usage and pricing insights and fold them into an existing product-wiki page — cited, dated, delivered as a PR. Use when the owner says "/explore-link <url>", or hands over a link and asks for it to be read into the wiki.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own — research it against the vendor's live documentation, capture what is portable as a technology skill with declared checks, and wire the project's use of it as a task in its structural local pack. Use when asked to make a repo do something with a technology nobody there has used yet (host it on X, send through Y, publish to Z), or to "research how to do this correctly" and "create a skill" for it.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- releasing-a-cloudflare-site: How a site served from Cloudflare is released — the version contract, the guards that stop a release loop or a half-release, forcing one, rolling one back, and which parts of Cloudflare only a person can change. Use when changing the release task, the wrangler config or the analytics loader, and when a release parks.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. - searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- write-a-requirement-leaf: How a requirement leaf is written in the executable spec — the backtick-numbered one-liner with its detail collapsed under it, and which kind (surface snapshot, behavior, logic, saga, per-project, e2e singleton) its case takes. Use when adding or reshaping a requirement line in requirements.md.
- write-a-saga: How a saga case is written — a multi-step story captured as a golden storyboard or one animated APNG golden — steps, captions, frame budget, the real entry point, delay stripping and gesture marking. Use when authoring or changing a case under the saga kind.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, get the owner's approval of the plan itself — a line per step, the dependency graph, each link's automerge policy — before filing any of its issues, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- writing-wiki-pages: How a product-wiki page is written and grown — the Key insights header, citation, what a source actually supports (attribution, independent voices, public proxies), correction without deletion, the growth log, sample-data, when a pass writes nothing. Loaded for any edit under product-wiki/.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); when the change has an issue,
   the body carries `Closes #<issue>` on its own line.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --pr <pr>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --pr <pr>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it
   again. (1)
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read an issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- deterministic-expecteds: What makes a rendered expected byte-stable — the pinned clock, faked inputs, real fonts, fixed-duration pumps — and the per-stack rendering recipe (jsdom+satori for DOM products, Flutter golden files) with pixel-exact comparison. Use when writing a case, the render harness or the fake world under dev/requirements.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- explore-link: Mine one given URL for product, market, usage and pricing insights and fold them into an existing product-wiki page — cited, dated, delivered as a PR. Use when the owner says "/explore-link <url>", or hands over a link and asks for it to be read into the wiki.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. - learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own — research it against the vendor's live documentation, capture what is portable as a technology skill with declared checks, and wire the project's use of it as a task in its structural local pack. - merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. - releasing-a-cloudflare-site: How a site served from Cloudflare is released — the version contract, the guards that stop a release loop or a half-release, forcing one, rolling one back, and which parts of Cloudflare only a person can change. - repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. - writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list.
